During this period, the mother rarely leaves the den for extended intervals, subsisting on food brought by the father or other pack members. This dietary transition is energetically demanding, and the timing of weaning is influenced by local prey availability and the condition of the lactating female. In resource-poor years, weaning may be delayed, which can have cascading effects on litter survival and subsequent female reproductive output.

This reproductive suppression, mediated by behavioral and hormonal cues, ensures that only the most competitively advantaged individuals contribute to the gene pool during any given season.

The species exhibits slight sexual dimorphism, with males generally exceeding females in body mass by roughly 10 to 15 percent across most of its geographic range.
